Senate Democrats had conditioned their votes on reforms to ICE following the January deaths of two U.S. citizens during federal enforcement operations in Minnesota. The final bill did not include those reforms. ICE and CBP will be funded separately through reconciliation.

That's an important data point. The shutdown was real and caused hardship for roughly 260,000 DHS employees. But it did not stop immigration enforcement operations in the way a full DHS shutdown would have. The enforcement data didn't pause, it kept accumulating.

The bill funds most of DHS (TSA, FEMA, the Coast Guard) but does not include ICE or CBP. Those agencies have separate funding streams, including from the 2025 reconciliation bill, which kept their enforcement operations largely running throughout the shutdown.

The DHS partial government shutdown that began February 14 ended April 30 (75 days) when Congress passed and Trump signed a bipartisan funding bill. That's the longest agency shutdown in U.S. history. It's worth understanding what it did and didn't affect.

Nagel's piece is a sharp, accessible primer on why current enforcement looks the way it does. Read it here: scholarcommons.sc.edu/geog_f… and for ongoing data-grounded analysis of how these policies play out: austinkocher.substack.com/p/…
The H1B fight between Miller and Musk isn't just a culture war spat. It's the perennial contradiction in U.S. immigration politics: restrictionist ideology meets employer demand for foreign labor.
Nagel's key insight: mass deportations like Operation Wetback (1954–55) and Depression-era expulsions of 2 million people of Mexican origin didn't reduce labor dependence on Mexican workers.

Stephen Miller's agenda is more radical than standard Republican restrictionism. Conservative pro-business politics have long supported H1B visas, 85,000 three-year visas/year for credentialed workers. Miller wants to gut that too.

The tension Nagel identifies is real: the U.S. has never fully embraced or rejected immigration. Legal admissions haven't dropped below 640,000 annually since 1988, including during Trump's first term.

American immigration restriction isn't a Trump innovation, it's a 150-year pattern of selectively deciding which foreigners are "worthy" of rights. Caroline Nagel's new piece in The Geographical Journal puts the current moment in that longer context, and it's worth reading.

Read the Journal: sciencedirect.com/science/ar… 
My substack: austinkocher.substack.com

The dataset has real limitations the authors acknowledge: county policies are mostly absent, the study ends in 2021, and the second Trump administration's wave of enforcement legislation isn't captured yet. That's exactly the gap that makes extending this data urgent.

Three anti-sanctuary states used financial penalties to prevent localities from enacting sanctuary policies. That mechanism ( threatening local budgets to enforce state policy) is becoming more common under the current administration.

Most local sanctuary ordinances (21 of 24) were passed during the first Trump administration. Most state anti-sanctuary laws were passed during the Obama years. States appear to act as a check on the federal government, whichever party holds it.

The geographic pattern is sharp. Anti-sanctuary laws were concentrated in the South, with 17 of 27 enacted there. Sanctuary laws concentrated in the West. Local sanctuary ordinances skewed Northeast; 15 of 24 city ordinances were in Northeastern cities.

The Drexel team identified 340 total policies(288 local and 52 state) enacted over that period. By 2021, more than half of all U.S. states had enacted either a sanctuary or an anti-sanctuary law. That's a significant shift in the legal landscape in roughly one decade.

A new pre-proof in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine does something that's been needed for a long time: a systematic legal mapping of sanctuary and anti-sanctuary policies across all 50 states and hundreds of localities from 2000 to 2021. Worth reading carefully.

Detention Report: detentionreports.com

Detention data is a good example. Counts change daily. A snapshot from last week may not reflect today's population. The number matters, but so does knowing exactly when it was pulled and from which agency report.

The tools Poynter highlights draw on government data; ICE ERO arrest figures, detention population counts, removal records. The data is real. The question journalists should always ask: what time period does this cover, and what isn't captured?

Poynter spoke with me about the current landscape. My read: we have better and more creatively sourced immigration data than ever before and we're also in a Wild West moment where many people are working with datasets they've never touched before.

More immigration data tools exist now than at any point in U.S. history. That's genuinely useful. It also creates real risks for journalists who use those tools without understanding their limits. Poynter's Jon Greenberg  digs into both sides.
